titleStmt.title: An improved LLF scheduling for reducing maximum heap memory consumption by considering laxity time

analytic.title: An improved LLF scheduling for reducing maximum heap memory consumption by considering laxity time

div.p: Real-time embedded systems are often designed as multiprocessor systems in order to achieve both low power consumption and high-performance. Also, they are often implemented as multitasking systems in order to meet deadline constraints of response times for multiple external inputs. However, multitasking systems often increase heap memory consumption allocated for temporal use, because the allocated memories for tasks often remain allocated simultaneously when the tasks are suspended for switching to the other task. In order to reduce memory consumption in real-time multitasking, in this paper we propose an improved real-time scheduling algorithm based on LLF (Least Laxity First) to reduce maximal heap memory consumption by controlling multitask scheduling, without modifying the processing order of each task. The proposed algorithm firstly performs LLF schedulability analysis (proposed in [5]) in each scheduling cycle and then switches between LLF and our proposed Least Memory Consumption First (LMCF) scheduling policies appropriately according to the analysis result. The proposed LMCF scheduling assumes that the amount of the heap memory allocation in the next step near future for each task can be predicted and according to the prediction it selects the least ones as many as the number of the processors for schedule. We evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm by comparing the heap memory reduction ratio of the proposed algorithm with that of LLF scheduling.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Typical examples of embedded systems include smartphones, household electric appliances, and medical equipment. Since these are often mass-produced, it is important to reduce manufacturing costs. Therefore, reducing memory consumption in embedded software development is one of the major development objectives [1].

In many embedded software, in order to improve responsiveness to multiple external inputs, there are often implemented as multitasking systems that perform concurrent processing by switching between multiple tasks. However, multitasking systems often increase heap memory consumption allocated for temporal use, because the allocated memories for tasks often remain allocated simultaneously when the tasks are suspended for switching to the other task. Therefore, in general, the heap memory consumption of the multitasking system tends to be larger than that of the single task system which realizes the same function.

A few scheduling methods for reducing memory consumption have been proposed [2], [3]. [3] proposed a memory reduction technique for the deterministic concurrent programming language SHIM. In [2], the behavior of each communication buffer is modeled for static analysis and discover combinations of buffers that can be shared by that model. However, since concurrent processing is used, the number of combinations of states of tasks becomes so large to analyse for practical large-scale systems. Some products that operate on multitasking systems that are actually on the market may handle 10 to 100 tasks. For those products, switching to other tasks increases heap memory consumption. Also, even if each single task has only a few states, the number of entire system states increases when the system is executed as a multitasking system since there is a possibility of taking all combinations in the state of each task. These existing proposals for memory savings are based on static analysis and all these are suffering from such state-space explosion when the systems scale becomes large. Instead of static analysis, it would be useful if we could reduce memory consumption in dynamic on-line scheduling.

On the other hand, real-time embedded systems are often designed as multiprocessor systems in order to achieve both low power consumption and high-performance. In multiprocessor systems, it is well-known that the LLF (Least Laxity First) scheduling giving priority from the task with the smallest laxity time is more optimal than the EDF (Earliest deadline First) scheduling [4] giving priority from the earliest task of the deadline [5].

In order to reduce memory consumption by dynamic online scheduling, in this paper, firstly we propose LMCF (Least Memory Consumption First) scheduling algorithm to reduce maximal heap memory consumption by controlling multitask scheduling, without modifying the processing order of each task. LMCF scheduling assumes that for each task, the number of the heap memory allocation increases (negative number for heap memory decrease) in the next step near future can be predicted, and according to the prediction it selects the least ones for schedule. Using LMCF scheduling, we can avoid reaching the worst case state where all the tasks allocate the maximum number of heap memories if it is avoidable.

Secondly, we propose an improved real-time scheduling algorithm by combining LLF and LMCF. The proposed algorithm firstly performs LLF schedulability analysis in each scheduling cycle and then switches between LLF and our proposed LMCF scheduling policies appropriately according to the analysis result. As a result of schedulablity analysis, when it is determined that all the tasks have some laxity in deadlines, LMCF scheduling is performed, and when they does not, LLF scheduling is performed.

We evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm by comparing the worst case memory consumption (WCMC in short) of the proposed algorithm with that of LLF scheduling. To do so, we calculate and compare the average memory reduction ratio of the number of deadline miss occurred of the proposed and compared (LLF) scheduling algorithms by the experimental simulation using randomly generated task sets.

div.head: II. LLF SCHEDULING AND SCHEDULABILITY ANALYSIS
div.p: In multiprocessor systems, LLF scheduling is more optimal than EDF scheduling [5]. For example, consider three tasks scheduling problem. Deadline and WCET (Worst Case Execution Time) of Task 1, Task 2, and Task 3 are 3, 2, 2 and 3, 1, 1, respectively. Suppose that in this scheduling problem, two processors are available, and the performance of both processors is equivalent. The result of applying EDF scheduling to this problem is shown in Fig. 1a The rectangle in the figure shows the processing task, and the identifier of the allocated processor is written. The upward arrow indicates the release time, the downward arrow indicates the deadline, and the horizontal axis indicates the time. In EDF scheduling, Task 2 and Task 3 are preferentially allocated to processors. However, as a result, Task 1's deadline is missed.

The result of applying LLF scheduling to the same problem is shown in Fig. 1b. Let i denote the time, L(i) denote the laxity time of each task, D(i) denote the relative deadline of each task, and C(i) denote the remaining execution time of each task. L(i) is calculated by Equation (1). As a result of calculating the laxity time of each task from Equation (1), the laxity times of Task 1, Task 2, and Task 3 are 0, 1, 1, respectively. In LLF scheduling, Task 1 and Task 2 are preferentially allocated to processors. Therefore, deadline miss of Task 1 can be avoided. Furthermore, after the completion of Task 2 processing, Task 3 can be allocated to the processor, and the scheduling problem is solved.

Since it is shown that there are no task sets that are schedulable in EDF but not in LLF, LLF scheduling is more optimal than EDF scheduling in multiprocessor systems. At time i, whether LLF scheduling satisfies the deadline constraint can be determined by calculating the excessive computing power of the processors in order to meet the deadlines [5]. First, let T j be the jth task. Next, let m be number of tasks, the laxity time of task j is calculated from Equation (1) and use the integer k(> 0) to classify the task into three sets.
div.formula: R 1 (k) = {T j | D j ≤ k} R 2 (k) = {T j | L j ≤ k ∩ D j ≥ k} R 3 (k) = {T j | L j ≥ k} R 1 is
div.p: a set of tasks whose processing must be completed within k unit time, R 2 is a set of tasks in which laxity time runs out in k unit time, and R 3 is a set of tasks that still have laxity time after k unit time passed. Let n be number of processor and the excessive computing power F (k, i) of the processors in order to meet the deadlines within k unit of time after the current time i is calculated by Equation (2).
div.formula: F (k, i) = k × n - Tj ∈R1 C j (i) - Tj ∈R2 (k -L j (i))(2)
div.p: If F (k, i) is greater than or equal to 0 for any integer k(> 0), the task set is LLF schedulable at time i [5]. When all the tasks are included in R 1 at a certain k, all the tasks must also be included in R 1 at subsequent k's. Therefore, in practice, it is enough to check schedulability until the time all the tasks are finished. Let D max be the maximum value of the deadline of the task to be scheduled. Then, the task set is LLF schedulable at time i if F (k, i) is greater than or equal to 0 for any k ranging over 0 < k ≤ D max .

div.head: III. LEAST MEMORY CONSUMPTION FIRST SCHEDULING
div.p: In this section, we define the proposed LMCF scheduling algorithm to reduce heap memory consumption during multitask execution. We firstly describe LMCF scheduling for single processor environment, and later we discuss its extension to the multiprocessor environment and its combination to other scheduling policies.

div.head: A. Least Memory Consumption First Scheduling for Single Processor Environment
div.p: In each scheduling cycle, LMCF compares the next step memory consumption increase of each task and gives priority to the task with the smallest memory consumption increase.

It may take huge computation time and thus it is not practical to check all the states from the initial state to the final state and to optimize so as to go through the optimal route with the smallest memory consumption. Therefore, the proposed LMCF scheduling just checks the next state of the current state for each task at every scheduling cycle, and the task with the smallest memory consumption increase is selected and scheduled. An example of concurrent processing of two tasks is shown in Fig. 2. Fig. 2 shows all changes in memory consumption during multitask execution, using two tasks Task 1 and Task 2 in the figure. Arrows in the figure indicate state transitions, the case where Task 1 (Task 2) is scheduled is shown by the lower left (right, respectively) arrows.

When the multitasking system in Fig. 2 is executed, assuming that it is processed by an arbitrary OS scheduler, there is a possibility of transitioning to the state having the maximum memory consumption 9 on the route from the initial state to the final state. On the other hand, the state transition in the case of scheduling based on LMCF is shown in Fig. 3. From Fig. 3, it can be seen that the state with the maximum memory consumption 9 can be avoided in LMCF. The theoretical correctness of LMCF scheduling is stated as follows: Definition 1. A task T i denotes a finite state machine that changes the state from the first step to e i (the final) step, and s ij denotes the state of the task T i at the jth step.

A task set T S is defined as T S = {T 1 , T 2 , T 3 , . . . , T n } and a state of a task set T S is defined as a (Cartesian) product of the state of each task, that is, (s 1j1 , s 2j2 , s 3j3 , . . . , s njn ). Let j i be a natural number ranging over 1 ≤ j i ≤ e i , the initial state of T S be the product of the initial states of all tasks T i (=state s i1 ) and the final state of T S be the product of the final states of all tasks T i (=state s iei ). For any state (s 1j1 , . . . , s iji , . . . , s njn ) of T S, the next state when T i is scheduled is defined as (s 1j1 , . . . , s i(ji+1) , . . . , s njn ). The amount of maximum memory consumption MaxMem(T S) and the maximum memory consumption state set MaxMStates(T S) of T S are defined as follows:
div.formula: MaxMem(T S) =max (s1j 1 ,...,sij i ,...,snj n ) {M (s 1j1 , . . . , s iji , . . . , s njn )} MaxMStates(T S) =argmax (s1j 1 ,...,sij i ,...,snj n ) {M (s 1j1 , . . . , s iji , . . . , s njn )}
div.p: The amount of maximum memory consumption for schedule S of a task set T S is defined as MaxMem(T S, S) = max (s1j 1 ,...,sij i ,...,snj n )∈S {M (s 1j1 , . . . , s iji , . . . , s njn )}.

A schedule visiting the maximum memory consumption states is defined as a schedule of T S that includes some state in MaxMStates(T S). A next state by LMCF scheduling of an arbitrary state (s 1j1 , . . . , s iji , . . . , s njn ) of T S is defined as the next state scheduled for task i such that Equation (3) holds:
div.formula: m(s iji ) = min 1≤k≤n m(s kj k )(3)
div.p: An LMCF schedule of T S is defined as a schedule of T S such that any state other than the initial state in the schedule is the next state by LMCF scheduling of the directly preceding state.
By the next theorem, we will show that we can always avoid the maximum memory consumption state by LMCF scheduling if it is avoidable.
Theorem 1. For any task set T S, no LMCF schedules of T S visit the maximum memory consumption states if there exists some schedule of T S that does not visit the maximum memory consumption states.

Proof. Assume that the theorem does not hold, that is, there exists an LMCF schedule S 1 that visits the maximum memory consumption state and a (possibly not LMCF) schedule S 2 that does not visit the maximum memory consumption state. We will prove that there exists a schedule S 3 such that MaxMem(T S, S 1 ) ≤ MaxMem(T S, S 3 ) ≤ MaxMem(T S, S 2 ) and hence it contradicts the assumption.

Let (s 1j1 , . . . , s iji , . . . , s njn ) be the first state from the initial state that is found common in the schedule S 1 and S 2 and its next state in S 1 is different from that in S 2 . Let T p and T q be the tasks that is scheduled in S 1 and S 2 at the state. Then, since m(s pjp ) ≤ m(s qjq ) holds from Equation (3), M (s 1j1 , . . . , s p(jp+1) , . . . , s njn ) = M (s 1j1 , . . . , s pjp , . . . , s njn ) + m(s pjp ) ≤ M (s 1j1 , . . . , s qjq , . . . , s njn ) + m(s qjq ) = M (s 1j1 , . . . , s q(jq+1) , . . . , s njn ) holds. This means that the total memory consumption of the next state of (s 1j1 , . . . , s iji , . . . , s njn ) in S 1 is always less than or to that in S 2 . Now, let S 2 be the schedule whose first part is the same as S 2 until the state (s 1j1 , . . . , s iji , . . . , s njn ), and the order of the rest part is changed from S 2 such that the order of T p 's schedule is advanced to just after the state (s 1j1 , . . . , s iji , . . . , s njn ). Then, by similar comparison as done for S 1 and S 2 above, the total memory consumption of the next state of (s 1j1 , . . . , s iji , . . . , s njn ) in S 2 is always less than or equal to that in S 2 . Also, the total memory consumption of the next state of (s 1j1 , . . . , s iji , . . . , s njn ) in S 1 is the same as that in S 2 since at this state the same task T p is scheduled in S 2 and S 1 .

Then now we focus on the next state (s 1j1 , . . . , s p(jp+1) , . . . , s njn ) when T p is scheduled, and compare S 1 with S 2 . Following the similar discussion above, we can construct S 2 such that the total memory consumption of the next state of (s 1j1 , . . . , s iji , . . . , s njn ) in S 2 is always less than or equal to that in S 2 , and the total memory consumption of the next state of (s 1j1 , . . . , s iji , . . . , s njn ) in S 1 is the same as that in S 2 . Iterating this construction until the final state is reached, we can finally obtain the schedule S 3 such that the total memory consumption at any state is less than or equal to the corresponding state of S 2 , and is equal to the corresponding state of S 1 . This means that MaxMem(T S, S 1 ) ≤ MaxMem(T S, S 3 ) ≤ MaxMem(T S, S 2 ) holds (actually equality holds for S 1 and S 3 ), and thus it contradicts the assumption that S 1 visits the maximum memory consumption state and S 2 does not. Hence the theorem is proved.

div.head: B. Least Memory Consumption First Scheduling for Multiprocessor Environment
div.p: Similar to the single processor case, in p processor environment, LMCF scheduling can be extended to giving priority to the p tasks with the smallest p memory consumption increases. The theoretical correctness in the multiprocessor case can be proved as follows.

div.head: Corollary 1. Theorem 1 still holds in a multiprocessor environment.
div.p: Proof. A reachable state set in multiprocessor scheduling is generally a subset of that of a single processor scheduling. For example, consider the case of two processors. For any state, a state s that can be reached when scheduling task T i and task T j at the same time and a state s that can be reached when scheduling task T i (or T j ) and then scheduling task T j (or T i ) sequentially are always equivalent.

That is, in the case of two processor environment, the state transition of two steps (excluding the case where the same task T i is scheduled twice consecutively since sequential processing cannot always be parallelized) may be regarded as one step. Similar discussion is possible for the case of p processors in general. Therefore, by the similar construction as Theorem 1 in such a more restricted state space than the single processor case, we can also construct a schedule S 3 that contradicts the assumption that the theorem does not hold.

div.head: C. Combination of Least Memory Consumption First Scheduling and Other Scheduling Policies
div.p: The simple LMCF scheduling tends to be trivial, that is, tasks are almost sequentially scheduled by the order of the amount of memory consumptions. However, such schedule does not enjoy the most of the benefit of multitasking, such as responsiveness. In many cases, combining LMCF scheduling with other scheduling policies is effective to make memory saving coexist with responsiveness. For example, by combining LMCF scheduling with round-robin scheduling policy, tasks are usually scheduled by LMCF and if some designated time has passed, the least recently scheduled task is forced to be scheduled in order to avoid starvation. In general, we call a scheduling policy such that at any scheduling cycle it determines to choose LMCF or other scheduling policy and perform the chosen one as partial LMCF scheduling. The formal definition of partial LMCF scheduling is as follows: Definition 2. For any task set T S, an enabling condition EC is defined as a function that takes a state of T S and returns a Boolean value (true or false). A partial LMCF schedule w.r.t. enabling condition EC is defined as a schedule of T S such that for any state (s 1j1 , . . . , s iji , . . . , s njn ) in the schedule that EC(s 1j1 , . . . , s iji , . . . , s njn ) is true, its next state is the same as the one by the LMCF scheduling.

For partial LMCF scheduling, we have the following weaker version of theoretical correctness result than Theorem 1: Theorem 2. For any task set T S and enabling condition EC, there exists a partial LMCF schedule of T S w.r.t. EC that does not visit the maximum memory consumption state if there exists some schedule of T S that does not visit the maximum memory consumption state.

Proof. Suppose that there exists a (possibly not LMCF nor partial LMCF) schedule S of T S that does not visit the maximum memory consumption state. We can construct a partial LMCF schedule S w.r.t. EC of T S by making the least memory consumption increase task first for schedule in any state (s 1j1 , . . . , s iji , . . . , s njn ) in S such that EC(s 1j1 , . . . , s iji , . . . , s njn ) = true. (Note that S is identical to S if EC(s 1j1 , . . . , s iji , . . . , s njn ) = false for every state.) The amount of memory consumption in any state in the obtained schedule S is clearly less than or equal to the corresponding state in S. Hence, S does not visit the maximum memory consumption state if S does not.

div.head: IV. LLF LMCF COMBINED SCHEDULING ALGORITHM
A. Summary
div.p: To make memory saving coexist with deadline guarantee, we propose LLF LMCF combined scheduling algorithm. The proposed algorithm firstly performs LLF schedulability analysis [5] in each scheduling cycle and then switches between LLF scheduling and our proposed LMCF scheduling policies appropriately according to the analysis result.

As a result of the LLF schedulability analysis, LMCF scheduling is performed when it is determined that scheduling becomes possible, and LLF scheduling is performed when it is determined that scheduling is impossible. In the following descriptions, we refer to the switching from LMCF to LLF scheduling as a schedule switching.

div.head: B. Scheduling algorithm
div.p: The proposed scheduling algorithm operates as follows. Firstly, F (k, i + 1) is calculated from Equation (2) for the current time i, the relative deadline D(i) of each task, and the laxity time L(i) of each task. Note that we assume that the scheduling cycle is the unit time of 1. Thus, i + 1 means the time after the next scheduling cycle.

It is determined that LLF scheduling is possible at time i+1, if F (k, i + 1) is greater than or equal to 0 for all integers k ranging over 0 < k ≤ D max , where D max is the time (maximum value of the absolute deadline of the task to be scheduled) at which all tasks have to be completed. Using the result of the LLF schedulability analysis, LMCF scheduling is performed if it is determined that LLF scheduling is possible at the next scheduling cycle, and LLF scheduling is performed if it is not, that is, some task will miss the deadline at the next scheduling cycle unless we perform LLF scheduling right now. Intuitively, the proposed scheduling algorithm performs LMCF scheduling if all tasks have some laxity for deadline, and switches to LLF scheduling if they do not.

We evaluate the computational time complexity of the proposed scheduling algorithm. The algorithm consists of the LLF schedulability analysis and the allocation of the processors to the tasks. The time complexity is O(m × D max ) in LLF schedulability analysis since the calculation time of F (k, i+1) is estimated as O(m) (m is the number of tasks) and must be calculated for all k's s.t. 0 < k ≤ D max . The time complexity is O(n × log m) in the allocation of the processors, since maximum of n tasks (n is the number of processors) are selected out of m tasks, and by devising the data structure, the time complexity of selecting the least memory consumption increase out of m tasks can be estimated as O(log m). Therefore, the total time complexity is O(m × D max ) + O(n × log m).

div.head: V. EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION A. Aims and Methods
div.p: In the evaluation experiment, we simulate the proposed algorithm for multiple randomly generated task sets. In order to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm we measure the worst case memory consumption (WCMC) and compare it with the case using the proposed algorithm and LLF scheduling. In this experiment, we change the number of tasks from 4 to 8, and set the number of processors to 2. Each task's release time, memory consumption increase for each state, and relative deadline are randomly generated according to the normal distributions. The combinations of average and standard deviation of the normal distribution for all the task parameters used in this experiment are shown in Table I. However, the relative deadlines in Table I are different parameters depending on the number of tasks to meet the deadline constraints in LLF. Moreover, since the schedulability of LLF LMCF combined is exactly the same as that of LLF, we filtered out the generated task sets that are not schedulable by LLF so that we can focus on the comparison of memory consumptions. As for the WCET of each task, the actual computation time under the experiment environment is measured 100 times beforehand and the average value is used. This is because it is difficult to strictly analyze the WCET of each task. In this experiment, the WCMCs of the proposed algorithm and LLF scheduling is measured, and the memory reduction ratio is calculated from the average value of the WCMCs. In addition, we measure the number of tasks that missed the deadline for each simulation. The CPU and OS used in the experiment are Intel(R) Xeon(R) CPU E5-2643 v2 @3.50GHz and Windows 7 Professional 64bit.

div.head: B. Results
div.p: Table II shows the average value of the WCMCs for the proposed algorithm and LLF scheduling, and its graph is shown in Fig. 4. Also, Table II shows the ratio of the number of the simulations that the scheduling algorithm is switched from LMCF to LLF, to the total number of the simulations. The memory reduction ratio was calculated from the average value of the WCMCs of the proposed algorithm and LLF scheduling. Table III and Fig. 5 show the memory reduction ratio. The experimental results in Fig. 4 show that in the case of scheduling 4 to 8 tasks with 2 processors, the proposed algorithm is able to reduce the memory consumption in all the cases compared with LLF scheduling. From Fig. 5, it can be seen that the memory consumption can be reduced on average in the proposed algorithm compared with LLF scheduling. Furthermore, it can be seen that as the number of tasks increases, the memory reduction ratio also increases. However, there were cases where the proposed algorithm could not reduce memory consumption.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: In order to reduce memory consumption in real-time multitasking, in this paper we proposed a novel memory-saving on-line scheduling algorithm called LMCF, and a real-time scheduling algorithm based on LLF and combined with LMCF to reduce maximal heap memory consumption. The proposed LLF LMCF combined algorithm makes memory saving coexist with deadline guarantee. Moreover, the proposed LMCF algorithm ensures to avoid the maximum memory consumption state in multitasking without time-consuming static analysis. Our experimental evaluation shows that the proposed algorithm can reduce memory consumption by about 15% to 20% in comparison with LLF scheduling in 2 processor environment.

The proposed algorithm assumes that the amount of the heap memory consumption in the next step near future for each task can be predicted. Such a prediction can be easily (but possibly inaccurately) done by recording the heap memory consumption of each program location of memory allocation during the previous execution, and using the information for the prediction of the current execution for the same program location. By using static program analysis like WCET analysis, the accuracy might be improved. Anyway, the prediction accuracy does not affect the schedulability but the memory effectiveness.
As future work, it is necessary to evaluate the proposed algorithm for increased number of processors with additional experiments, and to improve memory saving efficiency of the proposed algorithm.
